claims.text: A ferry schedule is governed by a delicate balance of passenger demand, route characteristics and operational constraints.
claims.label: the balance behind a schedule

claims.text: Building a schedule starts by analysing passenger traffic patterns drawn from historical data, seasonal trends and anticipated events such as holidays or festivals.
claims.label: passenger traffic analysis

claims.text: That analysis determines how often a ferry runs and how large a vessel is needed for the expected passengers and vehicles.
claims.label: service frequency and vessel size

claims.text: Shallow waters, narrow channels or prevailing winds can dictate slower speeds and force reduced service intervals.
claims.label: shallow water and narrow channels

claims.text: Ferry companies must also allow for loading and unloading time, terminal turnaround time and delays caused by weather.
claims.label: loading and turnaround time

claims.text: Operators track weather forecasts, vessel locations and passenger boarding numbers with monitoring systems that use predictive algorithms to anticipate bottlenecks and adjust schedules.
claims.label: real-time monitoring and prediction

claims.text: Strong storms or high tides can compel a temporary suspension of service for safety reasons.
claims.label: suspending service in storms
